Jeevan, you asked why I don't talk about my twenties. Sit. I'll tell you.
At twenty-four I walked away from a group I'd given four years to. People think leaving is the hard part. It isn't. The hard part is after.
I missed them. Isn't that strange? The singing, the shared meals, knowing exactly what to think. And I was ashamed, too. I'd told my own brother he was lost. I'd skipped my grandmother's funeral because they said family was a distraction.
For the first year I didn't know what music I liked. I'd stand in a shop and freeze. A counsellor told me, 'Just try things. Keep what you like.' So I did. Old film songs, it turned out. Cricket, again. Cooking fish badly.
What helped most was people. Your grandmother. My brother, who forgave me in one afternoon. Friends who argued with me about everything.
It took years, beta. But I came back to myself. Your Anirban Mama came back.

Bidisha's first job interview in three years was at ten; the auto broke down at nine-forty, and she arrived sweaty, holding her file like a shield. The panel asked the question she had dreaded: "What about this gap?"
She had practised with her counsellor. "I was part of a group that turned out to be controlling. I left last year, and I'm rebuilding." Her cheeks burned. She was ashamed of the years she'd believed their leader. But the woman on the panel only nodded and moved on to spreadsheets.
Afterwards Jomon, her old college friend, took her for coffee. He ordered for himself and waited. She stared at the menu for a long time. For years someone else had decided even this.
"I think... I like cold coffee," she said, surprised.
She still missed the group sometimes, the singing, the shared meals, and that grief could still ambush her. But today she had told her own truth and chosen her own drink.

qa.a: The gap.

qa.a: She felt ashamed of the years she believed the leader, even while bravely telling the truth.

His mother never mentioned it. She just kept putting poha on the table every morning, the way he had liked it as a boy.
On Saturday his old college friend Salma dragged him to a quiz night at a café. There were students, a retired judge, a woman who fixed motorbikes. Nobody agreed about anything. Someone argued that Nagpur oranges were overrated, and Nilesh laughed so hard he surprised himself.
Walking home, he realised he had formed an opinion about oranges without checking whether it was allowed. It felt small and enormous at once.
